source_text:
Fragmentum in epistulam ad Philemonem (in catenis)
Phm
1,1 Ἐν πολλαῖς ἐπιστολαῖς ξένον τίθησι ῥῆμα τοῦ μέλλοντος εἰσάγεσθαι λόγου
κατασκευαστικόν, καὶ νῦν ἐπειδὴ ἔμελλεν ἀξιοῦν ὑπὲρ Ὀνησίμου τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ἀξίᾳ–
ἀξία δὲ αὐτοῦ τὸ δεδέσθαι–, τὸ ἀξιόπιστον τῆς παρακλήσεως δείκνυσιν.
thought_title: Paul's unusual word prepares his appeal
orientation: Severianus is explaining how Paul opens the letter to Philemon, where Paul is about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus.
pass_a_gloss: In many letters he places an unusual word, preparatory of the argument about to be introduced, and now since he was about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus by his own worth—and his worth is being in chains—he shows the credibility of the appeal.

choices.why: The glossary fixes this rendering for the rhetorical term; it avoids the banned alternatives and keeps the sense of a striking, non-ordinary word.
The glossary requires this rendering; it captures the constructive, building-toward function of the word for the coming argument.
The glossary fixes this rendering for the petition on behalf of Onesimus; it preserves the verbal force of asking rather than claiming worth.
The glossary requires this rendering; it keeps the sense of Paul's claim to consideration without importing 'dignity' or 'merit'.
The glossary fixes this rendering for Paul's imprisoned state; it preserves the concrete sense of binding that grounds his worth.
Both glossary terms are used; 'credibility' renders ἀξιόπιστον and 'appeal' renders παρακλήσεως, matching the fixed English for each.

pass_b_english: In many of his letters Paul places an unusual word at the start, one that is preparatory for the argument he is about to introduce. Here too, since he was about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus, he shows the credibility of his appeal through his own worth—and his worth is being in chains.
